boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Boonville record (June 17, 1861) in Operations to Control Missouri [June-October 1861]. Lyon's June 13-15 move to Jefferson City and his later march south are context. Campaign-wide marches, returns, reinforcements and multi-action loss totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. Imported numerical estimates remain unchanged; this pass does not validate them as simultaneous opening forces.

claims.value: The frozen force field gives the Union about 1,700 and the State Guard no figure; the live field reads US 1,700 and CS 0. Lyon's June 22 report gives his whole command at about 1,700 and says the Governor had collected three or four thousand men at Boonville. Snead says Lyon left St. Louis with about two thousand men and moved on Boonville with about seventeen hundred, that Lyon expected at least three or four thousand, and that Marmaduke went out with between 400 and 500 men, Lyon greatly overestimating his strength.
claims.rationale: Figures of different populations and dates (Lyon's moving column, the Governor's assembled force, the detachment Snead says was engaged). The CWSAC 1,700 matches Lyon's own report, whose basis is not stated; the match is not corroboration. None is adopted as a matched opening strength. The live CS zero is not measured absence.

claims.value: Lyon's June 22 report puts his landing about 6 miles below Boonville; his June 30 report and Snead put it about eight miles below. Lyon says the State troops held for a while in the shelter of a house and a thicket of wood behind it, while his approach brought him onto high and open ground where most of his casualties occurred; Snead places the stand under cover of some buildings and a dense wood.
claims.rationale: Ground described by an interested report and a participant history; the two Lyon reports differ on the landing distance. No map verification.

claims.rationale: Transport and post-action delay from an interested report and a history; not a supply return for the engagement.

claims.value: The frozen commanders are Colonel John S. Marmaduke and Brigadier General Nathaniel Lyon; NPS says Marmaduke commanded on the field. Snead says Governor Jackson ordered Marmaduke out over his protest and then ordered him back to the city to join Parsons. Lyon's report describes his own landing and advance.
claims.rationale: Command roles from a participant history and an interested report. The Governor's orders are attributed as Snead gives them; the listed commanders do not receive automatic sole credit.

claims.value: The frozen and live results read Union victory. Lyon says the enemy were soon routed, their camp taken and Boonville occupied. Snead calls it a trifling engagement but a stunning blow to the Southern Rights people of the State.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit. Snead's assessment of consequences is campaign context, not the tactical result.

claims.value: The frozen casualty text reads 81 (US 31; CS 50); the live field reads 31 (US 31; CS 0). Lyon reports 2 killed, 1 missing and 9 wounded (two since dead), about 60 prisoners released on oath and the enemy's loss unknown. Snead gives the Federal loss as two killed and nine wounded and the State troops' as two killed and five or six slightly wounded.
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap.

open_questions: Blair's, Totten's and the State Guard reports, returns for Lyon's column and maps remain deferred.

NPS/CWSAC (the live battle page and the frozen Arnold rows) is one family. Thomas L. Snead's The Fight for Missouri (Scribner, 1886) is a retrospective history by the Missouri State Guard's acting adjutant-general and Price's chief of staff, who says he was with the Governor at Booneville and Carthage; it quotes Sigel's, Schofield and Sturgis's and Price's reports and is not independent of them. Lyon's June 22 and June 30, 1861 reports are one family of interested Union accounts. Official Records volumes are shared containers, not additional witnesses. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
